title: Self-Hosted Model Operations Capstone
summary: This intermediate module enables learners to design and evaluate a provider-neutral operating plan for a self-hosted model service. After completing it, learners can connect service objectives, monitoring, output validation, staged release, rollback, and incident evidence in one reviewable plan.
objectives: Define observable service and output acceptance criteria for a self-hosted model service.
Design a staged release plan with explicit pause and rollback conditions.
Distinguish infrastructure health signals from checks of model output acceptability.
Assemble an operations plan that another operator can evaluate before a release.
Explain which source citation changed in this update and which parts of the module that correction affects.

sections.title: Level and scope
paragraphs: This is an intermediate module. It assumes familiarity with basic service deployment concepts, request handling, logs, metrics, and the difference between testing and production operation. It introduces the operating-plan structure needed for the exercise and does not assume advanced reliability engineering or model research knowledge.

A self-hosted model service is treated here as a service whose deployment, monitoring, release decisions, and recovery procedures are controlled by the operating team. The module is provider-neutral and does not prescribe a product, tool, version, configuration key, hardware design, or numerical performance target.

sections.title: Source update
paragraphs: The previous item cited content/modules/self-hosted-model-operations/self-hosted-model-operations-capstone.json. That citation had an unregistered publisher and had never been verified, so it could not serve as an independently reviewable source.

This update replaces that citation with canonical material on service objectives, monitoring, release engineering, and model reporting. The correction affects the provenance of the module's guidance about measurable objectives, operational signals, controlled releases, and documented model evaluation. The instructional scope remains focused on the same self-hosted model operations exercise, and no unsupported numerical threshold, tool recommendation, version, or configuration key has been introduced.

sections.title: Define acceptance before release
paragraphs: Begin by stating what acceptable operation means. A service-level indicator is a measured property of service behavior, while a service-level objective sets a target for that indicator. The cited Service Level Objectives chapter explains why objectives should be expressed through measurable service behavior rather than a vague statement that the service should be reliable.

For this exercise, write acceptance criteria in two categories. Service criteria cover observable behavior such as successful request handling, latency, and resource saturation. Output criteria cover whether responses remain suitable for the service's intended use. The module does not supply numerical thresholds because none are established by the supplied material. The operating team must select and approve thresholds for its own workload before a release decision.

Document the model's intended use, evaluation conditions, relevant limitations, and known areas of weak performance. Model Cards for Model Reporting supports recording this context so that a reviewer can interpret evaluation results rather than treating one aggregate result as sufficient evidence.
sections.callout: A service can be available while producing unacceptable outputs. Operational acceptance therefore requires both service signals and output checks.

sections.title: Build an observation plan
paragraphs: Choose signals that let an operator distinguish user-visible failure from internal warning signs. The cited Monitoring Distributed Systems chapter identifies latency, traffic, errors, and saturation as central signals for service monitoring. A model service plan can use these categories without committing to a particular monitoring product.

For each selected signal, record what is measured, where the observation comes from, how it relates to an acceptance criterion, and who reviews it. Avoid collecting a signal merely because it is available. A useful signal must help an operator decide whether to continue, pause, investigate, or roll back.

Keep output validation separate from infrastructure monitoring. Infrastructure observations can reveal slow requests, failures, or constrained capacity, but they do not by themselves establish that model responses remain appropriate for the intended use. Output checks must use examples and evaluation criteria tied to that intended use.

sections.title: Stage the release and prepare recovery
paragraphs: A release plan should limit exposure while evidence is gathered. The cited Release Engineering chapter describes controlled, repeatable release practices and the value of reducing manual variation. In this exercise, divide the release into review points rather than changing the entire service without an intermediate decision.

Before beginning, record the evidence required to advance, the conditions that require a pause, and the conditions that require rollback. Also identify the previously accepted deployment or operating state to which the service can return. A rollback condition must be tied to an observable acceptance criterion so that the decision does not depend only on intuition during an incident.

The plan must also explain how operators will confirm recovery. Reverting a change is an action, not proof of recovery. After rollback, operators must check the same relevant service and output criteria that revealed the problem.

sections.title: Assemble the operating plan
paragraphs: Create one reviewable plan containing the intended use, workload assumptions, service acceptance criteria, output acceptance criteria, observation sources, staged release sequence, pause conditions, rollback conditions, recovery checks, and responsible decision roles. The plan should make clear which evidence is available before release and which evidence will be gathered during operation.

Review the plan by tracing one hypothetical failure from detection to recovery. Identify which signal reveals the problem, which acceptance criterion it violates, who makes the decision, what action follows, and what evidence confirms recovery. If any link is missing, revise the plan before treating it as operationally ready.

After completing this process, a learner can do more than list monitoring and deployment concepts separately. The learner can produce an integrated operating plan in which each release decision is supported by observable service behavior, output evaluation, and a defined recovery path.

sections.title: Evaluate the result
paragraphs: A complete submission is internally consistent. Every acceptance criterion has an observation method, every release stage has an advance or stop decision, every rollback condition points to a recovery action, and every recovery action has a confirmation check.

A reviewer should reject a plan that relies only on infrastructure health to establish output acceptability, introduces unapproved thresholds during the release, or names rollback without explaining how recovery will be verified. The reviewer should also flag workload assumptions or intended-use claims that lack documented evidence rather than silently treating them as facts.

questions.prompt: What changed in the source update described by this module?
choices: An unverified local file citation was replaced with canonical sources supporting service objectives, monitoring, release engineering, and model reporting.
A new monitoring product and version were mandated.
A numerical latency threshold was added for every deployment.
The module was changed from intermediate to advanced.
questions.explanation: The source-update section identifies the unverified local file citation and explains that canonical sources replaced it. No product, version, or universal numerical threshold was added.

questions.prompt: Which two categories of acceptance criteria does the module require?
questions.explanation: The module separates observable service behavior from checks that model outputs remain suitable for the intended use.

questions.prompt: Why are healthy infrastructure signals insufficient to approve a model service release?
choices: They do not by themselves establish that model outputs are acceptable for the intended use.
They cannot reveal latency or request failures.
They always require a named commercial product.
questions.explanation: Infrastructure monitoring can reveal service behavior, but output acceptability requires separate evaluation tied to intended use.

questions.prompt: What must happen after a rollback to establish that recovery succeeded?
choices: Operators must check the relevant service and output acceptance criteria again.
Operators must assume the previous state is healthy.
Operators must choose new thresholds during the incident.
Operators must remove all monitoring signals.
questions.explanation: Rollback is an action rather than proof of recovery. The operating team must confirm recovery against the criteria that revealed the problem.
